title: Coptic and Ge'ez Catholics
hook: Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea have their own Catholic churches

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chaldeans of Iraq, who still pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Your line was the language of jesus. Did you say talitha cumi to yourself? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

An official from Ethiopia is riding home in a chariot, reading aloud from the prophet Isaiah, and he can't make sense of it. A stranger runs alongside and asks whether he understands what he's reading. How can I, the man says, unless someone shows me? That stranger is Philip, and the story is in the Acts of the Apostles. By the end of the chapter, the man has asked to be baptized at water beside the road, and he goes on his way rejoicing. Africa is already in the story, in the New Testament itself. Today, the Catholics of Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea, whose churches have deep roots in that soil.
screen: `A CHARIOT, AND ISAIAH ALOUD.` → `HOW CAN I, UNLESS SOMEONE SHOWS ME?` → `AFRICA, FROM THE OPENING PAGES.`

segments.voice: Egypt comes first. Matthew's Gospel says an angel told Joseph, in the Douay-Rheims, "Arise, and take the child and his mother, and fly into Egypt." So the Holy Family were refugees in Egypt. Egyptian Christians, called Copts, treasure that, and tradition says the evangelist Mark later brought the Gospel to Alexandria. Beside the Coptic Orthodox Church stands a smaller community, the Coptic Catholic Church, which prays in the same Coptic tradition, using Coptic and Arabic, and is in communion with Rome. Next, Ethiopia and Eritrea. Acts calls the man in the chariot "a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch," a royal treasurer. Ethiopian Christians honor him, and their own tradition tells of the faith arriving at the royal court long ago. Their ancient church language is Ge'ez, with its own script, still used in prayer even though it's no longer spoken at home. Here, too, there is an ancient Orthodox church, and alongside it are two Catholic churches: the Ethiopian Catholic Church and the Eritrean Catholic Church, both praying in the Ge'ez tradition. Then what that tradition looks and sounds like. Drums and sistrums in the liturgy. Long fasts. White shawls. Priests carrying hand crosses that people kiss for a blessing. Last, a word about those Orthodox neighbors. These Catholic churches share a great deal with them: the language, the music, the saints, the fasts. What differs is communion with the bishop of Rome. The Catholic Church speaks of these Orthodox churches with deep respect, and prays for full unity, not for one to swallow the other.
screen: `FLY INTO EGYPT.` · `COPTIC CATHOLICS, ON THE NILE.` · `GE'EZ: THE PRAYER LANGUAGE OF ETHIOPIA.` · `SHARING NEARLY EVERYTHING WITH THE ORTHODOX.` · then, large: `A MAN OF ETHIOPIA, AN EUNUCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn toward the Horn of Africa. Settle, and breathe. Picture highlands and dry plains, a church cut into rock, a market at noon, a family on the move because of drought or war. Then picture the man in the chariot, reading and puzzled, and the stranger who ran to help him. If you pray, you can pray for Ethiopia, Eritrea and their neighbors, and for Egypt too, in your own words. If you don't, hold the people of that region in your attention, with respect. The bell holds the time.
Coptic and Ge'ez Catholics. The Eastern Catholic churches of Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea, sharing the ancient traditions of their Orthodox neighbors and in communion with Rome. Today's word.
Your line: africa's ancient churches. Today, be the one who asks, do you understand what you're reading, and then stays to help. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Coptic Catholics celebrate the liturgy in the Alexandrian tradition in Coptic and Arabic; Ethiopian and Eritrean Catholics celebrate it in the Ge'ez tradition, with Ge'ez and local languages, sharing music, fasts and feasts with their Orthodox neighbors.

what it means: Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea have Eastern Catholic churches with ancient traditions shared with their Orthodox neighbors.

what a scholar hears: the Coptic Catholic Church follows the Alexandrian rite; the Ethiopian and Eritrean Catholic Churches follow the Ge'ez (Alexandrian-derived) rite; both share these with the Coptic and Ethiopian Orthodox.

notes: The Coptic Catholic Church is described as 'a smaller community' beside the Coptic Orthodox Church; no numbers given. Confirm.
Tradition of Mark bringing the Gospel to Alexandria, and of the faith arriving at the Ethiopian royal court (Frumentius, Aksum), given without dates and marked as tradition. Confirm.
Liturgical description (drums, sistrums, long fasts, white shawls, hand crosses) is a general picture of Ge'ez-tradition worship; confirm it applies to the Catholic churches too.
'The Catholic Church speaks of these Orthodox churches with deep respect, and prays for full unity, not for one to swallow the other': confirm the summary of Catholic ecumenical teaching is fair.
Acts 8:31 ('How can I, unless someone shows me?') paraphrased, not quoted. Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 2:13 and Acts 8:27: confirm.
Original left null: no Ge'ez or Coptic spelling was verifiable.
